narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimated an 81% likelihood that you will leave your current position — well above the 40% threshold that triggers a promotion denial. This means the system flagged you as a high flight risk, which led to this outcome.

The strongest factor driving this prediction is your overall work experience of 6–10 years. While nearly half of promoted employees have only 1–5 years of experience, your longer career history appears to signal, in combination with other factors, a greater readiness or inclination to seek opportunities elsewhere.

Closely related is how long you have been with this specific organization — 1–5 years. This relatively short tenure here, paired with your broader experience, suggests to the model that you may not yet have deep roots in this role, making departure more likely.

The third contributing factor is that you have received other job offers while working here. This is notably uncommon — only about 1 in 5 promoted employees reported the same — and it meaningfully reinforces the prediction that you may be considering leaving.

All three factors pushed in the same direction: toward leaving.

As a next step, it would be worth having an open conversation with your manager or HR about your career development path and what a realistic promotion timeline looks like for you. Demonstrating a longer-term commitment to the organization — for instance, by engaging more deeply in internal projects or expressing your intentions to stay — could help shift this assessment in your favor during the next review cycle.
